name: Listwise softmax over user impressions
problem: The objective is pointwise logloss but GAUC and nDCG@5 are ranking metrics computed within a user. Pointwise training spends capacity calibrating absolute probabilities that the metric never reads.
approach: Group each batch by user_id (Encoded.user_id). For each user's impression list, apply a softmax over scores and maximise the log-likelihood of the positive items: L = -sum_pos log(exp(s_i) / sum_j exp(s_j)). Gradient w.r.t. logits is (softmax_prob - normalised_target), which slots straight into model.grad().
when: First thing to try. The objective/metric mismatch is the single clearest structural flaw in the baseline.
key_insight: Within-user softmax is exactly the quantity nDCG rewards: it only cares about relative order inside a user's list, matching the evaluation protocol.
paper: Cao et al., Learning to Rank: From Pairwise Approach to Listwise Approach, ICML 2007

name: BPR pairwise ranking loss
problem: Same objective/metric mismatch as listwise, but with a cheaper and lower-variance gradient.
approach: Within each user, sample (positive, negative) impression pairs and minimise -log(sigmoid(s_pos - s_neg)). dz is +/- sigmoid(-(s_pos - s_neg)) on the two rows. Only users with 0 < positives < impressions contribute, which is exactly the GAUC population.
when: Alongside or instead of listwise softmax. Directly optimises the pairwise ordering GAUC measures.
key_insight: GAUC is literally a pairwise ordering statistic, so a pairwise loss optimises the metric almost verbatim.
paper: Rendle et al., BPR: Bayesian Personalized Ranking from Implicit Feedback, UAI 2009

name: LambdaRank nDCG-weighted pairs
problem: Plain BPR treats every misordered pair equally, but nDCG@5 only cares about the top of each user's list.
approach: Weight each pairwise gradient by |delta nDCG| -- the change in the user's nDCG@5 from swapping that pair. Pairs that move items across the top-5 boundary dominate; pairs deep in the list contribute almost nothing.
when: After a pairwise loss is working. It is a refinement of BPR, not a replacement.
key_insight: The position discount means a swap at ranks 1-2 matters far more than one at ranks 40-41; the loss should reflect that.
paper: Burges, From RankNet to LambdaRank to LambdaMART: An Overview, MSR 2010

name: Attention over user behaviour history (DIN)
problem: The current encoding has no behavioural sequence at all. Each impression is scored independently of everything else the user has watched, despite hundreds to thousands of interactions per user in train.
approach: For each row, build the user's prior long_view history from the TRAIN split only, strictly before the current time_ms. Represent the candidate as an attention-weighted sum of history item embeddings, keyed by the candidate video/author. Truncate history to the most recent N (50-100).
when: Highest-value feature work. The organisers call this direction completely blank.
key_insight: A user's interest is multi-modal; attention lets the candidate item select which slice of history is relevant instead of averaging it all together.
paper: Zhou et al., Deep Interest Network for Click-Through Rate Prediction, KDD 2018
caution: History must be built causally -- only interactions strictly earlier than the row being scored, and only from train. Leaking future behaviour inflates validation and collapses on test.

name: Mean-pooled recent history features
problem: Same gap as DIN, but attention is a large step from a numpy FM.
approach: Add fields derived from the user's last N long_view items: most-frequent author, most-frequent tab, mean duration bucket. These enter as ordinary categorical fields that cross with the candidate under the FM.
when: A cheaper first step toward sequence modelling than full attention.
key_insight: Even a crude history summary crosses with candidate item fields, and crossing is the only channel through which user-side information can move a within-user ranking.
paper: Covington et al., Deep Neural Networks for YouTube Recommendations, RecSys 2016
caution: Causal construction only, same as DIN.

name: Auxiliary feedback heads
problem: long_view is the only signal used, while is_click, is_like, is_follow, is_comment, is_forward and play_time_ms sit unused in the log. Positives are sparse.
approach: Add auxiliary prediction heads over shared embeddings for one or more feedback columns via Split.feedback(). Total loss = main ranking loss + lambda * sum(auxiliary losses), with lambda small (0.1-0.3) so the scored task dominates.
when: After the ranking loss is in place, as a regulariser on the shared embeddings.
key_insight: Related feedback signals share structure; predicting them jointly denoises the embedding table without changing what is scored.
paper: Ma et al., Modeling Task Relationships in Multi-task Learning with Multi-gate Mixture-of-Experts, KDD 2018
caution: Feedback columns are TARGETS. Feeding one in as an input feature leaks the label -- features.py raises on this.

name: ESMM-style funnel over click then long_view
problem: long_view is conditioned on a click having happened, so the two signals form a funnel with sample-selection bias.
approach: Model P(long_view) = P(click) * P(long_view | click), training both factors over the full impression space rather than the clicked subset only.
when: After simpler multi-task variants. Worth testing whether the click->long_view funnel actually holds in this data before investing.
key_insight: Training the conditional factor only on clicked rows biases it; the product formulation trains everything on all impressions.
paper: Ma et al., Entire Space Multi-Task Model, SIGIR 2018

name: Censored watch-time regression (CWM)
problem: play_time_ms is truncated when a video ends, so it is right-censored. Squared error on a censored variable is biased, and long_view is itself a threshold on watch time.
approach: Use a one-sided loss: penalise under-prediction fully, but penalise over-prediction only when play_time_ms < duration_ms (that is, when the observation was not truncated). Use the resulting watch-time estimate as an auxiliary target or directly as a ranking score.
when: A research-depth direction with a real published result behind it.
key_insight: A video watched to completion tells you the true interest was AT LEAST that long, not exactly that long -- a censored observation, not a point estimate.
paper: Zhan et al., Counterfactual Watch Model / CWM (github.com/hyz20/CWM)
caution: The reference implementation pins torch==1.6.0 and reconstructs its own long_view2 label. Borrow the loss formulation, not the code.

name: Duration-bucket debiasing (D2Q)
problem: Watch-time signals correlate strongly with video duration, so a model can rank by duration rather than by interest.
approach: Bucket by duration and normalise the target within each bucket (e.g. rank-percentile of watch time inside its duration group) so the objective compares like with like.
when: If diagnostics show predictions tracking duration_ms more than user preference.
key_insight: Comparing raw watch time across a 10s and a 5min video measures video length, not interest.
paper: Zhan et al., Deconfounding Duration Bias in Watch-time Prediction, KDD 2022

name: Recency-weighted training samples
problem: Train spans 04-08 to 04-21 but test is 04-29 to 05-08, an 8-to-21 day gap. User interest and the item catalogue drift over that window.
approach: Weight each training row by exp(-(t_max - t) / tau) on its date, and tune tau on validation. Recent behaviour gets more influence.
when: Cheap to implement and directly addresses a structural property of the split.
key_insight: The split is chronological, so the training distribution is systematically older than the evaluation distribution.
paper: Standard practice; see Ding et al., Sampling-bias-corrected Neural Modeling, RecSys 2019

name: Time-of-day and day-of-week fields
problem: hourmin and date are in the log but unused. Short-video consumption is strongly diurnal.
approach: Add hour-of-day (from hourmin) and day-of-week (from date) as categorical fields so they cross with item fields under the FM.
when: Cheap. But note these are user-context, not item, fields.
key_insight: Time-of-day only helps through its cross with item features -- a term constant within a user's session cannot reorder that user's list.
paper: n/a -- standard feature engineering
caution: If a time field is near-constant within a user's impressions, its first-order term contributes exactly zero to a within-user ranking.

name: Randomised-exposure validation set
problem: The standard logs are biased by the deployed recommender. A model can overfit that policy's exposure distribution and look better offline than it is.
approach: Score against log_random_4_22_to_5_08_pure.csv (1.18M rows of randomised exposure) as a secondary, unbiased validation signal. Use it to detect overfitting to logging policy, not as the primary selection metric.
when: As a diagnostic once a model beats the baseline, to check the gain is real.
key_insight: Randomised exposure breaks the feedback loop, so it estimates true preference rather than the logging policy's preferences.
paper: Gao et al., KuaiRand: An Unbiased Sequential Recommendation Dataset, CIKM 2022
caution: Selection must still be made on the official validation split; this is a cross-check only.

name: DeepFM / DCN / xDeepFM
problem: The FM captures only second-order interactions.
approach: Add an MLP tower over concatenated embeddings alongside the FM term, or an explicit cross network.
when: EXPLICITLY DEPRIORITISED by the organisers -- ranked below loss, sequence, multi-task and watch-time work. Capacity is measured not to be the bottleneck.
key_insight: Higher-order interactions only pay off when the data supports the capacity; at 1.14M rows it does not.
paper: Guo et al., DeepFM, IJCAI 2017

name: Adding more static feature fields
problem: n/a
approach: Adding the full 13-field CWM static set (music_id, video_type, upload_type, plus six coarse user-side buckets).
when: NEVER. The organisers measured this: primary 0.5940 against 0.5950 for the current 5 fields. Within noise, slightly worse.
key_insight: user_id x video_id crossing already absorbs most of the learnable signal, and coarse user buckets are redundant given user_id.
paper: Starter Kit README, measured ablation

name: Increasing embedding dimension
problem: n/a
approach: Raising k from 16 to 32 or beyond.
when: NEVER. The organisers measured k = 8/16/32 at 0.5895/0.5902/0.5887. Flat.
key_insight: 1.14M rows will not support more capacity; the bottleneck is the objective, not the model size.
paper: Starter Kit README, measured ablation

name: Pure user-side first-order features
problem: n/a
approach: Adding user-side features whose value is constant across that user's impressions, expecting a first-order gain.
when: NEVER as a standalone term. Measured to contribute EXACTLY zero.
key_insight: Ranking is computed within a user, so any term constant across that user's rows leaves the intra-group order unchanged. Verified: item_pop x user_bias scores identically to item_pop alone. User-side features act only through crosses with item-side features.
paper: Starter Kit README, measured

name: Hybrid pointwise + ranking loss
problem: A pure ranking loss discards the calibration signal that pointwise logloss provides, while pointwise logloss ignores the ordering the metric actually measures.
approach: Train on L = logloss + lambda * ranking_loss rather than swapping one for the other. Start lambda around 0.3-1.0 and tune it. Both terms produce a dz per row, so add them: dz = dz_pointwise + lambda * dz_ranking.
when: When a pure ranking loss is close to but not clearly better than a pointwise baseline.
key_insight: The two terms are complementary rather than alternatives: one calibrates the embedding table, the other orders within a user.
paper: Standard multi-objective practice; cf. Burges et al. RankNet/LambdaRank hybrid training

name: Blend model score with an item-popularity prior
problem: Item popularity alone scores 0.5807 valid primary -- 96.5% of the FM baseline -- from pure statistics. The FM may be underusing this signal for cold or rare videos where its embedding is poorly estimated.
approach: In features.py fit() -- which receives ONLY the train split -- compute a smoothed per-video long_view rate: (pos + prior*global_mean)/(impressions + prior), prior around 20. Store it on FeatureState. In transform(), look the rate up BY VIDEO ID and bucket it into a categorical field so the FM can cross it. Never read labels in transform(). This is train-only target encoding and is explicitly permitted by the leak guard's fit() scoping.
when: Cheap, and the ablation numbers say the popularity signal is unusually strong on this dataset.
key_insight: An item-side prior is a legitimate within-user ranking signal because it varies across the candidates a user sees -- unlike a user-side term, which is constant within the group and cancels.
paper: Standard shrinkage/empirical-Bayes practice
caution: Compute in fit() only. Reading long_view inside transform() reads the evaluation split's own answers and is blocked. Do NOT use video_features_statistic_pure.csv -- its counters span the test window.

name: BPR with a proper learning-rate sweep
problem: GAUC is a pairwise ordering statistic, so a pairwise loss is the objective matched exactly to it. Divergence below a random-scoring floor indicates a step-size problem, not a broken objective.
approach: Re-run the pairwise loss and sweep the learning rate across at least an order of magnitude. A pairwise or grouped gradient has a different scale from pointwise logloss, so a step size tuned for one objective is not tuned for the other. Set lr explicitly in the config rather than inheriting a default.
when: Whenever a pairwise loss diverges or underperforms -- sweep the step size before concluding the objective is wrong.
key_insight: Divergence below a random-scoring floor indicates a step-size problem, not a broken objective. Sweep before discarding.
paper: Rendle et al., BPR: Bayesian Personalized Ranking from Implicit Feedback, UAI 2009

name: Average predictions across several seeds
problem: A single model's embeddings are a high-variance estimate when the user-item matrix is sparse. Independent seeds of the same configuration can differ materially.
approach: Train K models (K=5) with different seeds on identical data and config, then average their PREDICTED SCORES (not their metrics) at inference. In train.py, wrap fit() to build K models and return an object whose predict() averages the K score vectors. Since only relative order matters, averaging raw logits is fine.
when: High priority and unusually low risk. It is orthogonal to every other technique -- it can be stacked on top of whatever objective wins.
key_insight: Variance reduction, not bias reduction. Averaging predictions smooths per-seed idiosyncrasies in rare-item embeddings, where a sparse model is least certain.
paper: Breiman, Bagging Predictors, 1996; standard practice in every Kaggle recsys solution
caution: Costs K times the training compute, which feeds the resource score. Average PREDICTIONS, not metrics.

name: Weight training rows toward the end of the train window
problem: Train covers 04-08 to 04-21; test covers 04-29 to 05-08. The gap between the end of training data and the start of test is 8 days, and the far end is 21 days. Short-video catalogues and user interests drift fast, so the training distribution is systematically older than the evaluation distribution. Validation (04-22 to 04-28) sits between them, so an idea that helps here should transfer.
approach: Weight each training row by exp(-(date_max - date) / tau) using the `date` column, and sweep tau over roughly {3, 7, 14} days. Multiply the per-row weight into dz before model.grad(). Nothing else changes.
when: Cheap, orthogonal to the objective, and directly addresses a structural property of the chronological split that no experiment has touched.
key_insight: The split is chronological by design. Recent behaviour is a better estimate of test-period behaviour than three-week-old behaviour, and uniform weighting implicitly asserts otherwise.
paper: Standard practice; cf. Ding et al., Sampling-bias-corrected Neural Modeling, RecSys 2019
caution: Down-weighting most of the data reduces the effective sample size, so very small tau will hurt. If tau=3 is much worse than tau=14, the drift is mild and this direction is closed.
